preamble: Rebecca Randall is a girl of ten being sent from her mother’s farm to live with two aunts she barely knows. Mr Jeremiah Cobb drives the stage coach that is taking her there.
extract:
The old stage coach was rumbling along the dusty road that runs from Maplewood to Riverboro. The day was as warm as midsummer, though it was only the middle of May, and Mr. Jeremiah Cobb was favoring the horses as much as possible, yet never losing sight of the fact that he carried the mail. The hills were many, and the reins lay loosely in his hands as he lolled back in his seat and extended one foot and leg luxuriously over the dashboard. His brimmed hat of worn felt was well pulled over his eyes, and he revolved a quid of tobacco in his left cheek.

When he was about to leave the post-office in Maplewood that morning, a woman had alighted from a wagon, and coming up to him, inquired whether this were the Riverboro stage, and if he were Mr. Cobb. Being answered in the affirmative, she nodded to a child who was eagerly waiting for the answer, and who ran towards her as if she feared to be a moment too late. The child might have been ten or eleven years old perhaps, but whatever the number of her summers, she had an air of being small for her age. Her mother helped her into the stage coach, deposited a bundle and a bouquet of lilacs beside her, superintended the "roping on" behind of an old hair trunk, and finally paid the fare, counting out the silver with great care.

"I want you should take her to my sisters' in Riverboro," she said. "Do you know Mirandy and Jane Sawyer? They live in the brick house."

Lord bless your soul, he knew 'em as well as if he'd made 'em!

"Well, she's going there, and they're expecting her. Will you keep an eye on her, please? If she can get out anywhere and get with folks, or get anybody in to keep her company, she'll do it. Good-by, Rebecca; try not to get into any mischief, and sit quiet, so you'll look neat an' nice when you get there. Don't be any trouble to Mr. Cobb.--You see, she's kind of excited.--We came on the cars from Temperance yesterday, slept all night at my cousin's, and drove from her house--eight miles it is--this morning."

"Good-by, mother, don't worry; you know it isn't as if I hadn't traveled before."

The woman gave a short sardonic laugh and said in an explanatory way to Mr. Cobb, "She's been to Wareham and stayed over night; that isn't much to be journey-proud on!"

"It WAS TRAVELING, mother," said the child eagerly and willfully. "It was leaving the farm, and putting up lunch in a basket, and a little riding and a little steam cars, and we carried our nightgowns."

All this had been half an hour ago, and the sun, the heat, the dust, the contemplation of errands to be done in the great metropolis of Milltown, had lulled Mr. Cobb's never active mind into complete oblivion as to his promise of keeping an eye on Rebecca.

Suddenly he heard a small voice above the rattle and rumble of the wheels and the creaking of the harness. At first he thought it was a cricket, a tree toad, or a bird, but having determined the direction from which it came, he turned his head over his shoulder and saw a small shape hanging as far out of the window as safety would allow. A long black braid of hair swung with the motion of the coach; the child held her hat in one hand and with the other made ineffectual attempts to stab the driver with her microscopic sunshade.

"Please let me speak!" she called.

Mr. Cobb drew up the horses obediently.

"Does it cost any more to ride up there with you?" she asked. "It's so slippery and shiny down here, and the stage is so much too big for me, that I rattle round in it till I'm 'most black and blue. And the windows are so small I can only see pieces of things, and I've 'most broken my neck stretching round to find out whether my trunk has fallen off the back. It's my mother's trunk, and she's very choice of it."

"You can come up if you want to; there ain't no extry charge to sit side o' me." Whereupon he helped her out, "boosted" her up to the front seat, and resumed his own place.

Rebecca sat down carefully, smoothing her dress under her with painstaking precision, and putting her sunshade under its extended folds between the driver and herself. This done she pushed back her hat, pulled up her darned white cotton gloves, and said delightedly:--

"Oh! this is better! This is like traveling! I am a real passenger now, and down there I felt like our setting hen when we shut her up in a coop. I hope we have a long, long ways to go?"

At this moment the thought gradually permeated Mr. Jeremiah Cobb's slow-moving mind that the bird perched by his side was a bird of very different feather from those to which he was accustomed in his daily drives. He put the whip back in its socket, took his foot from the dashboard, pushed his hat back, blew his quid of tobacco into the road, and having thus cleared his mental decks for action, he took his first good look at the passenger, a look which she met with a grave, childlike stare of friendly curiosity.
editorialCuts: Removed Rebecca’s long speech about her lunch and the brick house, which names four relatives this extract never introduces.
Removed the 338-word head-to-foot description of Rebecca, which is the passage’s best-known paragraph and stops the scene dead for a third of its length.
Removed the interrupted speech about what makes a journey, and the parasol exchange that runs into a quoted Wordsworth stanza and changes register.

RESTORED Mr Cobb’s reply to the mother’s question about the Sawyer sisters. Cutting it had left her asking "Do you know Mirandy and Jane Sawyer?" and then answering herself with "Well, she’s going there" — a question nobody replies to, and a Well that presupposes the reply.

Removed the mother’s aside to herself as the stage pulls away. Without the paragraph in which she is named as the watcher, "she said to herself" attached to the child, who had just spoken. A pronoun with the wrong antecedent is worse than a lost line.

RESTORED "Please let me speak!" she called. Cutting it had left Mr Cobb drawing up the horses OBEDIENTLY with no order anywhere in the extract to obey — the same fault as the unanswered question, running the other way: the reply survived and the prompt was cut. Found by the second read this passage’s tier requires and had never had.

DROPPED the closing paragraph, "Mr. Cobb made none of these generalizations". Its demonstrative points straight at the 338-word description, which is cut, so the extract’s last sentence denied the reader something the reader had never been given. Restoring the description instead would have taken the passage to 1,285 words, 35% over a short-set ceiling, to save thirty words; dropping the paragraph costs one question hook and ends the extract on the look the two of them exchange.

narratorialSignposting.closest: At this moment the thought gradually permeated Mr. Jeremiah Cobb’s slow-moving mind that the bird perched by his side was a bird of very different feather from those to which he was accustomed in his daily drives.
narratorialSignposting.reading: QUOTED IN FULL THIS TIME. The earlier record stopped this sentence with a full stop after "different feather", which is not where Wiggin stops it — a hand-typed copy of an artefact, validated against nothing until the gate for it was written. The sentence reports the change; it does not name the method, which is that almost everything the reader is given of the child arrives at the moment Mr Cobb notices it and in his terms: a small voice he takes first for a cricket, then a tree toad, then a bird; a small shape; a braid. The narrator hands the reader her NAME, in her mother’s mouth, long before it hands over a face, and never remarks that this is what it is doing.

authoringRead.openingReference: CLEAN, AND CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. The extract opens on "The old stage coach was rumbling along the dusty road that runs from Maplewood to Riverboro" and names Mr Jeremiah Cobb in the same paragraph. No pronoun, definite reference or demonstrative in the first paragraph points outside the extract. This is the control for the tier-0 amendment: contiguity is not what makes an opening safe, naming is.
authoringRead.seams: FOUR INTERNAL CUTS AFTER THE CHANGES, WALKED IN READING ORDER. 11->13 drops the first sight of the passenger; the join goes from Mr Cobb on the box to a flashback opening "When he was about to leave the post-office in Maplewood that morning", which carries its own time marker and introduces the child inside itself. Sound. 19->24 drops four paragraphs including the mother’s aside; the join lands on "All this had been half an hour ago", the source’s own resumption. Sound, and this is the cut whose earlier version produced the wrong-antecedent fault. 28->30 drops the attribution paragraph, so the driver’s reply follows the child’s speech with no "Mr Cobb waited until" between them; the speaker is recovered five words later by "Whereupon he helped her out". MARGINAL AND KEPT — an author should not write a who-said-it item on that line. 32->37 drops the parasol exchange; the join is "I hope we have a long, long ways to go?" -> "At this moment the thought gradually permeated...". The deictic "At this moment" outlived its original beat, but the beat it now attaches to is her question, which works.
authoringRead.secondRead: REQUIRED BY TIER 2 (four internal cuts) AND NEVER PERFORMED BEFORE THIS AUDIT. It found two faults, both of the class Addendum 28 names, in a passage already banked and already used for the twelve items of ENG-018. (1) "Mr. Cobb drew up the horses OBEDIENTLY" with nothing to obey. The paragraph before it had the child making ineffectual attempts to stab the driver with her sunshade; her actual call, "Please let me speak!", was the one paragraph cut between them. The adverb is the tell, and the fault is the mirror of the one this passage was already fixed for once: there a question survived and its reply was cut, here a reply survived and its prompt was cut. FIXED by restoring the six-word paragraph, at a cost of six words and one numbered line. (2) "Mr. Cobb made none of these generalizations" as the extract’s LAST SENTENCE, with the generalizations — the 338-word portrait — cut. A demonstrative pointing at removed text, in the position a reader remembers best. FIXED by dropping the paragraph. The alternative, restoring the portrait, was measured rather than estimated: 1,285 words against 917, roughly 35% over a short-set ceiling, to save a thirty-word paragraph the curation had already argued against on its own merits. COST OF THE FIX, STATED: one question hook is gone (the withheld reasoning), and the signposting reading that leant on it has been rewritten. Every numbered line from 43 onward moved by one, so ENG-018’s line references were re-pointed and its gates re-run rather than assumed.
authoringRead.pronounResolution: MANDATORY HERE — three of the four cuts remove a paragraph naming a person. Every paragraph-opening pronoun and every "said to herself" resolved against the extract alone. The mother’s "she" is fixed by "a woman had alighted" in the same paragraph; the child’s "she" at the nightgowns line is fixed by "said the child"; "he" at "All this had been half an hour ago" is Mr Cobb, named in the same sentence; "she" at "Please let me speak!" is fixed by the small shape hanging out of the window in the paragraph before. The dangerous one went with the mother’s aside, which is what the earlier fix removed. NOTE FOR AUTHORS: the mother is never named in the extract at all — she is "a woman", "her mother", "the woman". No item may ask for her name.
